newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia dlr lacks bounce, sellers continue to cap.
newsitem.headline: Australia dlr lacks bounce, sellers continue to cap.

text.p: The Australian dollar was unable to challenge resistance at US$0.7380 through the morning, but remained supported above US$0.7330 as the market waits on next week's second quarter inflation and wages data.

Traders said the fact that the dollar was consolidating just above the 18-month low of US$0.7310 reached earlier this week, without having a solid shortcovering bounce, suggested the market was comfortable with the lower value.
By noon (0200 GMT), the Australian dollar was trading at US$0.7359/64, up from an early US$0.7349/54, and just under Wednesday's US$0.7365/70 close.
"The fact that we haven't see a massive move up means the market probably is not that short, or they are comfortable being short," one trader said.

While the dollar was edging higher after a soft opening, there were plenty of sellers on rallies, and the brief overnight move above US$0.7380 had not triggered the shortcovering squueeze that had been expected.

The focus remains on next week's inflation and wages data, which is expected to show moderate inflation pressures and has led the market to expect, or in the case of the currency, fear a fifth cut in official interest rates.

On the crosses, the Australian dollar was at 85.38/48 yen, up from an early 85.14/24 but still down on Thursday's late 85.56/66. The story was Similar On The trade weighted index, with the midsession reading of 56.9 up a notch on the open, but just below Thursday's 57.0 close.
The fall in the New Zealand dollar, which dropped a cent overnight to reach a 19-month low of US$0.6767/72 today, had surprisingly little impact on the local dollar.
"The Kiwi's had a pretty horrible 24 hours, but there's been no flow through to the Aussie. The Kiwi just seemed to be a large one-off deal, somebody just getting out," one trader said.

While the Kiwi was off its lows, it remained under some pressure and although it had little direct impact on the Australian dollar, its weakness was not a positive for the unit. "Certainly with the Kiwi going down, it's going to be difficult for the Aussie to go up," the trader said.
